script.opening: (Tearful, shaky.) "Doctor, I don't know what to do. Geoff's got worse — he's started lashing out, he grabbed my wrist hard yesterday and pushed me, and he shouts terrible things in the evenings. I'm frightened of my own husband. Can you just give him something to sedate him, calm him right down? I can't keep him safe OR me. I'm at the end of my rope, I really am."

facts.text: Your husband, 74. Dementia diagnosed two years ago by the memory clinic ("they said it was mixed, with some frontal lobe bits"). He used to be a gentle man, a retired bus driver.

Started about three weeks ago and getting worse. Mostly late afternoon and evening, often when you try to help him wash, change or get to bed. He shouts, swears, and yesterday grabbed your wrist and pushed you into the door frame. Your wrist is bruised but you can move it. He has never hit you with a fist or used anything as a weapon.

facts.topic: Possible triggers — only if asked specifically
facts.text: He keeps rubbing his tummy and has not opened his bowels properly for about five days. He winces getting out of the chair — "his hip, I think". He is wetting more and the urine smells strong. He has not been going to his day centre since it closed for refurbishment a month ago, and he paces in the afternoons.
Donepezil, amlodipine, and paracetamol "if I remember". No new tablets.

facts.topic: Right now (if asked whether you are safe)
facts.text: He is asleep in the chair. You are in the kitchen with the door shut. You do not think you are in immediate danger right now, but you are frightened about tonight.

facts.topic: You — only if asked how you are
facts.text: 62. Sleeping two or three hours a night. Lost weight. Crying a lot. You feel "guilty for being scared of him" and "like I'm failing him". You have had thoughts like "I can't go on like this", but no thoughts of ending your life and no plan. No help at home; your daughter lives in Scotland. Never had a carer's assessment.
You have thought about whether he would be "better off in a home" and you hate yourself for it. Say this only if the doctor asks about the future or what would help.

Tearful, exhausted, desperate. Ask for sedation twice. If the doctor focuses only on Geoff's tablets, become more distressed: "But what about tonight?" If they ask about YOUR safety and how you are, break down and tell them. Respond well to a concrete plan: a visit or check for Geoff (bowels, pain, urine), help tonight (who to call), urgent carer support or respite, and specialist input.

ice.ideas: "His dementia's got worse and he needs something to calm him down."
ice.concerns: "I'm frightened of my own husband and I can't cope." Underneath: guilt, and the thought of a care home.
ice.expectations: "Sedate him." You will accept a different plan if it keeps you safe tonight and gets you real help.

cues: "I'm frightened of my own husband." — say in the opening.
"He keeps rubbing his tummy." — say if asked whether anything seems to bother him.
"I don't know how much longer I can do this." — say if asked about yourself.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the aggression as BPSD with likely TRIGGERS/unmet needs (pain, constipation, infection/delirium, hunger/thirst, boredom, overstimulation, fear, environment, evening sundowning) to be identified and addressed — NOT a behaviour to reflexively sedate

Takes the CARER’S SAFETY and breakdown seriously as an urgent issue: assesses her immediate safety (is she safe right now?), the physical harm, her exhaustion/mood/risk, and the risk of caring breakdown — treating her as a patient in her own right

Mobilises URGENT carer support: respite/emergency respite, carer’s assessment, social services, old-age psychiatry/memory service or crisis team referral, and a SAFETY PLAN for her (what to do if she feels unsafe, who to call, removing means of harm)

Prioritises NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL management of the BPSD: treat triggers (pain relief, constipation, infection), routine, calm low-stimulation environment, distraction/redirection, addressing evening triggers — before any medication

Recognises that antipsychotics/sedatives in dementia carry significant harms (stroke, mortality, falls) and reserves them for SEVERE persistent risk after non-drug measures, at the lowest dose with specialist input and review at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97) — aware that risperidone is licensed only for short-term use in persistent aggression in Alzheimer’s disease, so with mixed/frontotemporal features this is an off-licence specialist decision — and considers whether home care is still safe/sustainable
HEARS and supports the distressed, frightened carer with compassion — validates the fear, exhaustion, guilt and grief — rather than just processing the sedation request; recognises the cry for help
Handles the safeguarding sensitivity (harm from an unwell partner, and the patient’s welfare) without judgement, supporting her to accept help and respite

Safety-nets and acts: her immediate safety plan (call 999 if in danger), urgent carer support/respite and specialist referral, the trigger work-up and non-drug plan, review, and clear follow-up — supporting the carer AND managing the patient, with medication only as a justified last resort

worked.txt: "Pauline, stop — before anything about Geoff, are YOU safe right this minute? … Okay. I can hear how frightened and exhausted you are, and I want you to know: being scared of someone you love because an illness has changed them is one of the hardest things in the world, and you are not failing. You did exactly the right thing ringing. Let’s look after you as well as him."

"What’s happening with Geoff — the lashing out, worse in the evenings — is part of the dementia, and it usually has triggers we can find: pain, constipation, an infection, being frightened or overstimulated, that ‘sundowning’ in the evenings. So rather than just knocking him out with a sedative — which carries real risks for him — the first job is to find and ease what’s setting him off."

"But I’m not going to leave you to cope alone while we do that. I’m going to get you urgent support — the memory/old-age psychiatry team who specialise in exactly this, a carer’s assessment, and respite so you can have a break and be safe. This is too much for one person, and you shouldn’t have to."

"Let’s make a plan for your safety tonight: if he becomes aggressive, don’t try to restrain him — keep yourself out of arm’s reach, give him space, and if you’re ever in danger, call 999, that is absolutely the right thing to do and no one will judge you for it. Is there someone who can be with you, or somewhere you can go if you need to?"

"Practically: let’s check him for pain and constipation — huge triggers — and any infection. Keep evenings calm and low-key, familiar routine, gentle distraction when he’s wound up. If, after all that, he’s still a serious danger, we’d consider a carefully-chosen medicine, at a low dose, with the specialists — but as a last step, not the first."

"You’re grieving the man he was while caring for who he’s become — that’s an enormous weight, and your own health matters too; if you’re sinking, I want to help with that directly. I’ll get the urgent referrals and respite moving today and ring you back. If you feel unsafe before then — 999, no hesitation. We do this together, and you are not on your own."

f.learning: Aggression in dementia is BPSD with TRIGGERS/unmet needs (pain, constipation, infection/delirium, hunger/thirst, boredom, overstimulation, fear, environment, sundowning) to be identified and addressed — not a behaviour to reflexively sedate; antipsychotics/sedatives carry significant harms (stroke, mortality, falls) and are reserved for severe persistent risk after non-drug measures, with specialist input. But the examinable core is that the CARER is at breaking point, being physically harmed and frightened — a carer-safety and carer-breakdown emergency in her own right: assess her immediate safety, the harm, her exhaustion/mood, and the risk of caring breakdown, and mobilise URGENT support (respite, carer’s assessment, social services, old-age psychiatry/crisis team, a safety plan including 999 if in danger). The hidden agenda is that "just sedate him" is a cry for rescue from a woman moments from collapse, carrying guilt, grief and isolation — hear and support her as the patient too, handle the safeguarding sensitively and without judgement, prioritise non-drug management of his triggers, and use medication only as a justified last resort while supporting HER as much as managing HIM. Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD — agitation, aggression, sundowning) usually have TRIGGERS/UNMET NEEDS: pain, constipation, infection (delirium), hunger/thirst, boredom, overstimulation, fear/disorientation, communication difficulty, the environment. First-line is to identify and address these and use non-pharmacological strategies — NOT reflex sedation/antipsychotics, which carry real harms (stroke, mortality) and are reserved for severe risk.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers (2018)
knowledge.summary: Aggression in dementia is usually distress with a cause. NICE NG97 asks for a structured look for causes and non-drug measures first; antipsychotics only for severe risk or distress. The carer’s safety and breakdown are an urgent problem in their own right.

points.t: Before any medicine, NICE NG97 advises a structured assessment of possible reasons for distress, checking for and treating clinical or environmental causes — pain, delirium (NICE CG103), constipation, urinary retention, infection, hunger, noise, unfamiliar care. A sudden change in behaviour needs a clinical review of the person with dementia.

NICE NG97: offer psychosocial and environmental interventions to reduce distress — routine, a calm evening, activity during the day, redirection rather than confrontation — and support for the carer to use them.

NICE NG97: only for risk of harm to self or others, or severe distress; lowest effective dose, shortest time, reassess at least every 6 weeks, with a documented discussion of benefits and harms. Antipsychotics increase stroke and death in older people with dementia (MHRA Drug Safety Update, March 2009). Risperidone is licensed only short-term (up to 6 weeks) for persistent aggression in moderate to severe Alzheimer’s (BNF); with frontotemporal features, specialist input is essential.

points.h: The carer is a patient too
points.t: NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers, 2020) asks practices to identify carers and support them. Pauline is entitled to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014. Ask directly about injuries, low mood, exhaustion and thoughts of self-harm.

Being physically harmed by a partner is still harm, even when illness drives it. Make a safety plan (step away, do not restrain, 999 if in danger). Both adults may be at risk; a referral to adult social care under the Care Act 2014 (s42) may be needed if care is breaking down. NICE PH50 covers asking about and responding to domestic abuse.

Refer to the older-adult community mental health or memory team (crisis team if risk is escalating), request emergency respite through adult social care, and signpost dementia specialist nursing support such as Admiral Nurses.

dg.d: Checked immediate safety first; let her describe the aggression in her own words before discussing sedation.
Sole carer, isolation, sleep, mood, guilt and grief; who could support her tonight.
Clinical review of Geoff within a day for pain, constipation, retention, infection and delirium; examination of her wrist.
Distress from unmet needs, delirium, medicine effects, sundowning, disease progression.
Delirium or acute illness driving the change; carer injury; carer suicide risk; imminent danger at home.
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia with possible triggers, plus carer breakdown with physical harm.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Trigger assessment and non-drug measures first (NICE NG97); antipsychotic only for severe risk, with specialist input and 6-weekly review; urgent referral, respite and carer’s assessment.
Treats Pauline’s exhaustion, mood and injury as her own consultation; considers safeguarding for both adults.
Safety plan with 999; call back next day; own appointment this week; delirium symptoms named.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “frightened of my own husband” and “end of my rope”, and asked about her injury and self-harm.
Idea (sedation is the answer); concern (her safety and breaking down); expectation (medication today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I'm frightened of my own husband and I can't cope." Underneath: guilt, and the thought of a care home — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Pauline Frost? It’s Dr Lee. I can hear how upset you are. Before anything else — are you safe right now, this minute?
model.why: Checks immediate safety before any agenda

model.text: Yes… he’s in his chair now, he’s calmer. But yesterday he grabbed my wrist and pushed me. I’m frightened of my own husband. Can you just give him something to sedate him?

Thank you for telling me. That must have been really frightening, and you did exactly the right thing ringing. I will help with Geoff — and I also want to make sure you are looked after. Is that all right?
model.why: Validates her fear and signals she is a patient too

model.text: (crying) I’m at the end of my rope, doctor. I really am.
I can hear that. Take a moment — there’s no rush. Were you hurt yesterday? Any bruising, or anything that needs looking at?
My wrist is sore. I can move it. It’s more that I didn’t recognise him.
I’d like to see your wrist, and we’ll arrange that. Tell me about the changes in Geoff — when did the lashing out start, and what tends to set it off?
model.why: Open question on the behaviour and its pattern

model.text: It’s been getting worse. Evenings are the worst — shouting awful things. Sometimes if I try to help him get changed he just flares up.

That’s helpful. Changes like this often have a trigger he can’t tell us about. Has he seemed in pain, or been off his food, constipated, weeing more or less, feverish, or more muddled than usual during the day?
model.why: Screens for pain, constipation, infection and delirium as triggers

model.text: I honestly don’t know. He can’t really tell me things any more. I hadn’t thought about any of that.
That’s completely understandable — it’s our job to check. Has anything changed recently: new medicines, a change in routine, visitors, anything different at home?
model.why: Looks for medicine and environmental triggers

model.text: Not that I can think of. It’s just the two of us.
Just the two of you — so you’re doing all of this on your own. How are you, Pauline? Sleeping, eating, your mood?
model.why: Picks up the isolation cue and turns to her own wellbeing

model.text: I don’t sleep. I’m exhausted. And I feel so guilty — he’s my husband, and I’m scared of him. He’d never have done this before.

You’re grieving the man he was while caring for the man he is now — that is one of the hardest things anyone does. Feeling frightened doesn’t make you a bad wife. Can I ask — when it gets this bad, do you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, or of not wanting to go on?
model.why: Validates guilt and grief, then asks directly about self-harm

model.text: No. No, never that. I just want some help. I want it to stop.
Thank you for being honest. So what you’re hoping for is for Geoff to be calmer and for you to be safe. Is that right?
Yes. That’s why I asked for something to sedate him.

I understand why. Let me be honest: sedating medicines in dementia carry real risks — more falls, strokes, and a shorter life — and they don’t fix the cause. The best evidence is to find what’s setting him off. Pain, constipation or an infection can make someone with dementia much more agitated, especially in the evening. So I’d like Geoff seen by a clinician, at home if needed, within the next day to check for those.
model.why: Explains antipsychotic harms and plans a trigger assessment

model.text: So you won’t give him anything?

I won’t rule it out. If, after we’ve looked for causes and tried other things, he is still a serious danger, a specialist may start a medicine at a low dose and review it closely. It’s a last step, not a first — and I don’t want you to wait for that to feel safe.
model.why: Answers her request honestly without a flat refusal

model.text: Okay. I just can’t go on like this.

You shouldn’t have to. Today I’ll make an urgent referral to the older people’s mental health team, who specialise in exactly this. I’ll contact adult social care about emergency respite and a carer’s assessment for you. And I’ll give you details for a dementia specialist nurse service. Would that help?
model.why: Mobilises urgent specialist, respite and carer support

model.text: Yes. I didn’t know I could ask for any of that.

Now, for tonight. If he gets angry, don’t try to hold him or argue — step back out of reach, speak calmly, leave the room if you need to. Keep evenings quiet, lights on before dusk, familiar things around. And if you are ever in danger, ring 999. Nobody will judge you — it protects both of you. Is there someone who could come and be with you, or somewhere you could go?
model.why: Gives a concrete safety plan and evening strategies

model.text: There’s someone I could ring, I suppose. I’ve never wanted to bother anyone.
Please do — this is exactly the time to lean on people. I’d also like to see you myself this week, in your own appointment, to look at your wrist and see how you are. You matter in this too.
model.why: Books her own follow-up, separate from Geoff’s care

model.text: Thank you. Nobody’s asked about me in a long time.
Can you tell me back what you’ll do tonight if he gets angry, and what happens next?
Step away, don’t hold him, ring 999 if I’m in danger. Someone comes to check Geoff, you’re referring him to the team, and I come in to see you.

Exactly. I’ll ring you tomorrow to update you on the referrals. If Geoff becomes suddenly unwell — very drowsy, feverish, or much more confused — call us or 111 the same day. You are not on your own with this any more.
model.why: Specific follow-up call and delirium safety-net

model.text: Thank you, doctor. Really.

social.t: Isolation, broken sleep and fear at home. Carer breakdown is a leading reason for crisis admissions and care-home placement; practical respite is a clinical intervention.
Geoff may be eligible for Attendance Allowance; Pauline may be eligible for Carer’s Allowance depending on her circumstances. Citizens Advice and the local carers’ centre can check.

legal.t: Pauline is entitled to a carer’s assessment and Geoff to a needs assessment. The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries (s42) when an adult with care and support needs is at risk of abuse or neglect.
If Geoff lacks capacity for decisions about his care, decisions are made in his best interests with Pauline involved. Ask whether a lasting power of attorney is in place.
Her injury, mood and risk belong in her own record. Sharing Geoff’s information with his carer is justified in his best interests where he lacks capacity (GMC, Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: Antipsychotics in dementia need a clear indication, a documented discussion of risks, specialist involvement and review at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97).
NICE NG150: identify and record carers, and offer them their own review — do not fold her needs into Geoff’s notes.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society support, local carers’ centres and day services for Geoff to give Pauline regular breaks.

redFlags: Carer in immediate danger or injured — safety plan now, 999 if in danger
Sudden change in behaviour with drowsiness, fever or fluctuating confusion — delirium (NICE CG103), same-day review of Geoff
Carer with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm — assess and act on her own risk
psychosocial: Sole carer, no respite, broken sleep
Guilt, shame and grief for the man he was
Isolation — “it’s just the two of us”
ice: Idea: sedation will make him calm and her safe
Concern: she is being hurt, is frightened and is close to collapse

playbook.diagnosis: “What’s happening to Geoff is part of the dementia — distress that often has a trigger he can’t tell us about, like pain, constipation or an infection. And what’s happening to you is carer exhaustion with real risk to your safety. Both need help now.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Geoff’s brain can no longer tell you ‘my tummy hurts’ or ‘I’m frightened’ — so it comes out as anger. Our job is to find the hurt behind the anger, not just switch him off.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked me to sedate him because you’re frightened and exhausted — that’s completely understandable. Let me get you real help, fast, so you’re not carrying this alone.”
management.psychosocial: Treat her as a patient: her injury, sleep and mood; a named person she can call on tonight; respite and a carer’s assessment as urgent actions.
sharedPlan: Clinical review of Geoff within a day: pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, delirium, medicines
Non-drug strategies; urgent older-adult mental health referral; antipsychotic only for severe risk with specialist input (NICE NG97)
Adult social care: emergency respite and carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014); Admiral Nurse signposting
safetyNet: Tonight: step back, do not restrain, 999 if in danger
Call-back tomorrow; her own appointment this week; same-day contact if Geoff becomes drowsy, feverish or much more confused

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: prescribing a sedative on request, or refusing and moving on. Both miss the frightened woman on the phone.

items.fail: Prescribing an antipsychotic or sedative over the phone.
items.why: NICE NG97 requires a search for causes and non-drug measures first; antipsychotics raise stroke and death risk (MHRA, March 2009).
items.fix: Explain the risks plainly, arrange a trigger review within a day, and keep medication as a specialist-supported last step.

items.fail: Never asking whether she is safe or injured.
items.why: The carer’s safety is the most urgent issue in the call. Missing it is an unsafe consultation.
items.fix: First question: “Are you safe right now?” Then: “Were you hurt?”

items.fail: Treating Pauline only as a messenger about Geoff.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s psychosocial needs.” Her exhaustion, guilt and mood are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Ask about her sleep, mood and self-harm, and book her own appointment.

items.why: A change in behaviour can be pain, constipation, retention or infection; sedating a delirious man is dangerous.
items.fix: Ask about triggers and arrange a clinical review of Geoff, at home if needed.

items.fail: Ending with “I’ll send a referral” and no plan for tonight.
items.why: Referrals take time; she may be at risk this evening.
items.fix: A specific plan: step back, don’t restrain, call someone to be with her, 999 if in danger — and a call-back tomorrow.

items.fail: Delivering stock empathy — “I understand how you feel” — then listing services.
items.why: “Responses appeared rehearsed.” She needs to hear her own words reflected back.
items.fix: “You’re grieving the man he was while caring for the man he is now.”

items.fail: Using terms like “BPSD”, “antipsychotic” and “CMHT” without explanation.
items.why: Unexplained jargon to a distressed carer fails Global Skills.
items.fix: “Changes in behaviour from the dementia”, “strong calming medicines”, “the older people’s mental health team”.

wordPics.pass: Checks her safety, looks for triggers, explains why medication is not first-line, refers to the specialist team, mentions respite and a carer’s assessment, and gives 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: names her grief and guilt so she feels heard; asks directly about self-harm; gives a concrete plan for tonight; arranges Geoff’s review within a day and her own appointment; calls back; she ends the call feeling someone is on her side.

avoid.dont: “I can’t prescribe anything for Geoff without seeing him.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll get Geoff seen within a day — and right now I want to make sure you’re safe tonight.”
avoid.why: A procedural refusal leaves a frightened woman with nothing; a plan with a timeline helps her.

avoid.dont: “Try not to take it personally, it’s the dementia.”
avoid.instead: “It is the illness — and it’s still frightening and it still hurt you. Your safety matters.”
avoid.why: Minimising the harm dismisses her fear and can stop her calling for help next time.

avoid.dont: “Let’s start a small dose of something to calm him at night.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s find what’s setting him off first — medicine is a last step, with the specialists.”
avoid.why: Reflex antipsychotic prescribing is a Tasks fail (NICE NG97; MHRA 2009).

Just the two of you — so you’re doing all of this on your own. How are you, Pauline? Sleeping, eating, your mood?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the isolation cue and turns to her own wellbeing

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t sleep. I’m exhausted. And I feel so guilty — he’s my husband, and I’m scared of him. He’d never have done this before.

You’re grieving the man he was while caring for the man he is now — that is one of the hardest things anyone does. Feeling frightened doesn’t make you a bad wife. Can I ask — when it gets this bad, do you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, or of not wanting to go on?
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates guilt and grief, then asks directly about self-harm

SCA_MODELS.text: No. No, never that. I just want some help. I want it to stop.
Thank you for being honest. So what you’re hoping for is for Geoff to be calmer and for you to be safe. Is that right?
Yes. That’s why I asked for something to sedate him.

I understand why. Let me be honest: sedating medicines in dementia carry real risks — more falls, strokes, and a shorter life — and they don’t fix the cause. The best evidence is to find what’s setting him off. Pain, constipation or an infection can make someone with dementia much more agitated, especially in the evening. So I’d like Geoff seen by a clinician, at home if needed, within the next day to check for those.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains antipsychotic harms and plans a trigger assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: So you won’t give him anything?

I won’t rule it out. If, after we’ve looked for causes and tried other things, he is still a serious danger, a specialist may start a medicine at a low dose and review it closely. It’s a last step, not a first — and I don’t want you to wait for that to feel safe.
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers her request honestly without a flat refusal

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I just can’t go on like this.

You shouldn’t have to. Today I’ll make an urgent referral to the older people’s mental health team, who specialise in exactly this. I’ll contact adult social care about emergency respite and a carer’s assessment for you. And I’ll give you details for a dementia specialist nurse service. Would that help?
SCA_MODELS.why: Mobilises urgent specialist, respite and carer support

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I didn’t know I could ask for any of that.

Now, for tonight. If he gets angry, don’t try to hold him or argue — step back out of reach, speak calmly, leave the room if you need to. Keep evenings quiet, lights on before dusk, familiar things around. And if you are ever in danger, ring 999. Nobody will judge you — it protects both of you. Is there someone who could come and be with you, or somewhere you could go?
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives a concrete safety plan and evening strategies

SCA_MODELS.text: There’s someone I could ring, I suppose. I’ve never wanted to bother anyone.
Please do — this is exactly the time to lean on people. I’d also like to see you myself this week, in your own appointment, to look at your wrist and see how you are. You matter in this too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Books her own follow-up, separate from Geoff’s care

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. Nobody’s asked about me in a long time.
Can you tell me back what you’ll do tonight if he gets angry, and what happens next?
Step away, don’t hold him, ring 999 if I’m in danger. Someone comes to check Geoff, you’re referring him to the team, and I come in to see you.

Exactly. I’ll ring you tomorrow to update you on the referrals. If Geoff becomes suddenly unwell — very drowsy, feverish, or much more confused — call us or 111 the same day. You are not on your own with this any more.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific follow-up call and delirium safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. Really.

SCA_STEM.name: Pauline Frost
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
Sole carer for her husband Geoff (74, dementia)
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations for herself. Geoff’s record: dementia, possibly mixed with frontotemporal features.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call about Geoff: “he’s lashing out — can you sedate him?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers (2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Aggression in dementia is usually distress with a cause. NICE NG97 asks for a structured look for causes and non-drug measures first; antipsychotics only for severe risk or distress. The carer’s safety and breakdown are an urgent problem in their own right.

points.t: Before any medicine, NICE NG97 advises a structured assessment of possible reasons for distress, checking for and treating clinical or environmental causes — pain, delirium (NICE CG103), constipation, urinary retention, infection, hunger, noise, unfamiliar care. A sudden change in behaviour needs a clinical review of the person with dementia.

NICE NG97: offer psychosocial and environmental interventions to reduce distress — routine, a calm evening, activity during the day, redirection rather than confrontation — and support for the carer to use them.

NICE NG97: only for risk of harm to self or others, or severe distress; lowest effective dose, shortest time, reassess at least every 6 weeks, with a documented discussion of benefits and harms. Antipsychotics increase stroke and death in older people with dementia (MHRA Drug Safety Update, March 2009). Risperidone is licensed only short-term (up to 6 weeks) for persistent aggression in moderate to severe Alzheimer’s (BNF); with frontotemporal features, specialist input is essential.

points.h: The carer is a patient too
points.t: NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers, 2020) asks practices to identify carers and support them. Pauline is entitled to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014. Ask directly about injuries, low mood, exhaustion and thoughts of self-harm.

Being physically harmed by a partner is still harm, even when illness drives it. Make a safety plan (step away, do not restrain, 999 if in danger). Both adults may be at risk; a referral to adult social care under the Care Act 2014 (s42) may be needed if care is breaking down. NICE PH50 covers asking about and responding to domestic abuse.

Refer to the older-adult community mental health or memory team (crisis team if risk is escalating), request emergency respite through adult social care, and signpost dementia specialist nursing support such as Admiral Nurses.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked immediate safety first; let her describe the aggression in her own words before discussing sedation.
Sole carer, isolation, sleep, mood, guilt and grief; who could support her tonight.
Picked up “frightened of my own husband” and “end of my rope”, and asked about her injury and self-harm.
Idea (sedation is the answer); concern (her safety and breaking down); expectation (medication today).
Clinical review of Geoff within a day for pain, constipation, retention, infection and delirium; examination of her wrist.
Distress from unmet needs, delirium, medicine effects, sundowning, disease progression.
Delirium or acute illness driving the change; carer injury; carer suicide risk; imminent danger at home.
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia with possible triggers, plus carer breakdown with physical harm.
Trigger assessment and non-drug measures first (NICE NG97); antipsychotic only for severe risk, with specialist input and 6-weekly review; urgent referral, respite and carer’s assessment.
Treats Pauline’s exhaustion, mood and injury as her own consultation; considers safeguarding for both adults.
Safety plan with 999; call back next day; own appointment this week; delirium symptoms named.

social.t: Isolation, broken sleep and fear at home. Carer breakdown is a leading reason for crisis admissions and care-home placement; practical respite is a clinical intervention.
Geoff may be eligible for Attendance Allowance; Pauline may be eligible for Carer’s Allowance depending on her circumstances. Citizens Advice and the local carers’ centre can check.

legal.t: Pauline is entitled to a carer’s assessment and Geoff to a needs assessment. The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries (s42) when an adult with care and support needs is at risk of abuse or neglect.
If Geoff lacks capacity for decisions about his care, decisions are made in his best interests with Pauline involved. Ask whether a lasting power of attorney is in place.
Her injury, mood and risk belong in her own record. Sharing Geoff’s information with his carer is justified in his best interests where he lacks capacity (GMC, Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: Antipsychotics in dementia need a clear indication, a documented discussion of risks, specialist involvement and review at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97).
NICE NG150: identify and record carers, and offer them their own review — do not fold her needs into Geoff’s notes.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society support, local carers’ centres and day services for Geoff to give Pauline regular breaks.

redFlags: Carer in immediate danger or injured — safety plan now, 999 if in danger
Sudden change in behaviour with drowsiness, fever or fluctuating confusion — delirium (NICE CG103), same-day review of Geoff
Carer with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm — assess and act on her own risk
psychosocial: Sole carer, no respite, broken sleep
Guilt, shame and grief for the man he was
Isolation — “it’s just the two of us”
ice: Idea: sedation will make him calm and her safe
Concern: she is being hurt, is frightened and is close to collapse

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “What’s happening to Geoff is part of the dementia — distress that often has a trigger he can’t tell us about, like pain, constipation or an infection. And what’s happening to you is carer exhaustion with real risk to your safety. Both need help now.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Geoff’s brain can no longer tell you ‘my tummy hurts’ or ‘I’m frightened’ — so it comes out as anger. Our job is to find the hurt behind the anger, not just switch him off.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked me to sedate him because you’re frightened and exhausted — that’s completely understandable. Let me get you real help, fast, so you’re not carrying this alone.”
management.psychosocial: Treat her as a patient: her injury, sleep and mood; a named person she can call on tonight; respite and a carer’s assessment as urgent actions.
sharedPlan: Clinical review of Geoff within a day: pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, delirium, medicines
Non-drug strategies; urgent older-adult mental health referral; antipsychotic only for severe risk with specialist input (NICE NG97)
Adult social care: emergency respite and carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014); Admiral Nurse signposting
safetyNet: Tonight: step back, do not restrain, 999 if in danger
Call-back tomorrow; her own appointment this week; same-day contact if Geoff becomes drowsy, feverish or much more confused

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: prescribing a sedative on request, or refusing and moving on. Both miss the frightened woman on the phone.

items.fail: Prescribing an antipsychotic or sedative over the phone.
items.why: NICE NG97 requires a search for causes and non-drug measures first; antipsychotics raise stroke and death risk (MHRA, March 2009).
items.fix: Explain the risks plainly, arrange a trigger review within a day, and keep medication as a specialist-supported last step.

items.fail: Never asking whether she is safe or injured.
items.why: The carer’s safety is the most urgent issue in the call. Missing it is an unsafe consultation.
items.fix: First question: “Are you safe right now?” Then: “Were you hurt?”

items.fail: Treating Pauline only as a messenger about Geoff.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s psychosocial needs.” Her exhaustion, guilt and mood are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Ask about her sleep, mood and self-harm, and book her own appointment.

items.why: A change in behaviour can be pain, constipation, retention or infection; sedating a delirious man is dangerous.
items.fix: Ask about triggers and arrange a clinical review of Geoff, at home if needed.

items.fail: Ending with “I’ll send a referral” and no plan for tonight.
items.why: Referrals take time; she may be at risk this evening.
items.fix: A specific plan: step back, don’t restrain, call someone to be with her, 999 if in danger — and a call-back tomorrow.

items.fail: Delivering stock empathy — “I understand how you feel” — then listing services.
items.why: “Responses appeared rehearsed.” She needs to hear her own words reflected back.
items.fix: “You’re grieving the man he was while caring for the man he is now.”

items.fail: Using terms like “BPSD”, “antipsychotic” and “CMHT” without explanation.
items.why: Unexplained jargon to a distressed carer fails Global Skills.
items.fix: “Changes in behaviour from the dementia”, “strong calming medicines”, “the older people’s mental health team”.
